migrationNotes: Spine: a drinks machine is run through coin sequences until its states are seen to be defined by their jobs, the same idea is carried to minds and made many-sided by Putnam, and Searle's locked room then puts it to the test.

lesson.title: Function and the Chinese Room

lead.text: Picture two calculators on a desk. One is built from gears and levers and the other from silicon chips. Press 3 + 4 on each and both show 7. Inside they have nothing in common, and nobody hesitates to say that both are adding.

That shows something about the word. What makes a device an adder is what it does with the numbers it is given: the same inputs go in and the same sums come out. The material makes no difference. Plenty of everyday things are named this way. A thermostat is anything that switches the heating on when it gets cold, whether it is made from a metal strip or a chip, and a cashier is whoever takes the money at the till.

Philosophers call a thing's job in a system its function. An adder's function is to produce sums, and anything that performs that function counts as an adder. The question for this lesson is whether the same could be true of minds. To make the idea exact we first need a simple machine to study.
Think about what makes something an adder.

steps.headline: A drinks machine as a table

lead.text: The philosopher Ned Block used a drinks machine as his example. It sells a can for 20p and takes 10p and 20p coins. It starts with nothing owed. Everything it does can be written as a table, called a machine table. The table lists the states the machine can be in, here “nothing owed” and “10p credited”. For each state and each coin it says what the machine does next, which means the state it moves to and what comes out.

The rules are short. From nothing owed, a 10p moves the machine to 10p credited and nothing comes out. From 10p credited, a 10p completes 20p, so a can comes out and the machine goes back to nothing owed. A 20p from nothing owed buys a can at once. A 20p from 10p credited buys a can and returns 10p.

Notice what the table leaves out. It says nothing about gears, chips or springs. The state “10p credited” is whatever state of the machine turns a further 10p into a can, so a state is identified by its role in the table. Philosophers call this a functional state: a state defined by what it does with inputs and which state it leads to, whatever it is made of.
Use the table to decide what the state called “10p credited” amounts to.
Block's machine sells a can for 20p and starts with nothing owed. Follow the state after each coin, using the rules you have just read.

reveal.text: You ran the table: credit, can, credit again. The state “10p credited” is just whatever role it plays in the next move.

steps.headline: Run the machine on 10p, 20p, 10p from nothing owed. What has come out, and where does it end?

workedSteps.text: 10p from nothing owed: the machine moves to 10p credited. Nothing comes out.
20p with 10p credited: it pays for a can and returns 10p. The machine goes back to nothing owed.
10p again: it moves to 10p credited. In all, one can and 10p change have come out.

steps.headline: Start with nothing owed and insert 20p, then 10p, then 20p.

workedSteps.text: 20p with nothing owed buys a can at once.
Count the cans after the last coin.

steps.headline: The same table in different materials

lead.text: Now carry the idea over to minds. Functionalism is the view that a mental state is defined by its role in the system. Pain, on this view, is whatever state is caused by injury and in turn produces a wish for it to stop and a tendency to wince and withdraw.

That puts functionalism in competition with the identity theory of the last lesson, which said that pain is one particular brain state. Putnam objected in 1967 that pain seems to occur in humans and in octopuses, whose nervous systems are very different. It might one day occur in silicon too. If pain were one particular brain state, creatures without that state could not feel it. If pain is a role, anything that plays the role can feel it.

afterFigure.text: This is multiple realisability: the same table can be implemented by gears, neurons or chips, so one mental kind can have many different physical realisers. The drinks machine shows the pattern in small, and Putnam's claim is that minds show it too.

lead.text: Putnam used pain in humans, in octopuses and in possible robots as his examples. Name the thesis they support.

If functionalism is right, a machine that plays the right role has a mind. In 1980 John Searle set out to show that this cannot be so. Imagine him locked in a room with a slot in the wall. Slips of paper covered in Chinese characters arrive through the slot. Searle knows no Chinese, and to him the characters are meaningless squiggles. He has a rulebook in English that tells him which characters to pass back out for each batch that comes in.

To the people outside, the room holds a fluent Chinese speaker. They post questions and get sensible answers. Yet Searle understands nothing. He is following rules that connect shapes with shapes, and he has no idea what any of it means. The rulebook plays the part of a machine table, and Searle plays the part of the machine running it.

Searle concludes that running the right program cannot be enough for understanding. A program works on the shapes of symbols, which is syntax, while understanding needs meaning, which is semantics. His slogan is that syntax is not sufficient for semantics. He grants that the room behaves like a speaker of Chinese. What he denies is that behaving like one, by running a program, amounts to understanding.

Searle's argument drew many replies, and the best known is the systems reply. It agrees that the man understands no Chinese and says that this does not matter. The man is one part of a larger system that also contains the rulebook and the slips of paper, and the whole system is what understands. A single neuron in your brain understands no English either.

Searle answered that the man could memorise the whole rulebook and do the work in his head, so that the system would be inside him. He would still understand no Chinese. His critics reply that the memorised system might understand even though the man's ordinary self does not know it, and the two sides have not agreed.

So the disagreement turns on whether playing the right role is enough for a mind. Functionalism says yes. Searle says that the room shows otherwise. Neither side can point to a settled case, which is why the room is still discussed.
Some philosophers agree that the man in the room understands no Chinese, and still say that something in the room understands. Name their reply.

reveal.text: The systems reply says the whole room understands. Searle answers that he could memorise the rules and still understand nothing. His slogan: syntax is not sufficient for semantics.

lesson.orientation: Model a mental state by its causal role, see why one role can have many realisers and weigh Searle's Chinese Room.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: In a film, an android grips its arm and says that it is in pain. It flinches from the fire, keeps away from it afterwards and describes the pain as you would. Most viewers feel pulled two ways. The android behaves like something in pain, and it is made of metal and wire.

The last lesson ended with physicalists, who say the mind is physical. Some of them add that what matters about a mind is what it does, and what it is made of is beside the point. If they are right, a machine could in principle have a mind. If they are wrong, no machine could, whatever its behaviour.

This lesson starts with a drinks machine, which has no mind but shows plainly what it means to be defined by what something does. It then moves to the claim about minds, and ends in a locked room where a man answers questions in Chinese without understanding a word.

intro.promise: By the end you'll run a machine table, say why one mental state could have many physical realisers, and weigh Searle's Chinese Room.

recap.keyIdea: A mental state can be defined by its role, so one kind can have many realisers. Searle's room asks whether playing the right role is enough for understanding.

blocks.text: You ran Block's drinks machine on several coin sequences and saw that its table never mentions what it is made of. You then carried the idea to minds and met the room that tests it.

recap.nextHook: If a mind is a pattern of doing, the next question is what makes a pattern the same one over time. The next lesson asks what makes you the same person as the child in your oldest photographs.

questions.prompt: Ned Block's drinks machine sells a can for 20p, takes 10p and 20p coins and starts with nothing owed. Someone inserts 10p, then 10p, then 10p. How many cans come out?
hints: Track the state after each coin: nothing owed or 10p credited.
A can comes out only when the total reaches 20p.
Count the coins that complete a 20p total.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 10p sets a credit; the second 10p completes 20p and releases a can; the third sets a new credit. One can.

questions.onCorrect: One can: the first 10p sets a credit, the second buys a can, the third starts a new credit.

misconceptions.feedback: A can comes out when the credit reaches 20p. Track the state after each coin.
Not every coin buys a can. Track the state after each one.

questions.prompt: Ned Block's drinks machine sells a can for 20p and takes 10p and 20p coins. It starts with nothing owed. Someone inserts 20p, then 10p, then 20p. How many cans come out?
hints: A 20p coin with nothing owed buys a can immediately.
Track the credit left after each coin.
A 20p coin with 10p already credited overpays by 10p but still buys a can.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 20p buys a can at once; 10p sets a credit; 20p with 10p credited buys a can and returns 10p. Two cans.

questions.onCorrect: Two cans: the first 20p buys one at once, and the last 20p buys another after the 10p credit.

misconceptions.feedback: A 20p with 10p already credited overpays by 10p but still buys a can.
The 10p in the middle only sets a credit. Track the state after each coin.

questions.prompt: Name the thesis, used by Putnam against the identity theory, that a single mental kind such as pain can be realised in very different physical systems.
hints: Think of pain in humans, octopuses and possible robots.
The thesis says one kind can be 'realised' in many ways.
questions.onCorrect: Multiple realisability: one mental kind, many physical realisers.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a theory about mental states. The thesis wanted says one kind can be realised in many ways.

questions.prompt: Searle says the man in the room understands no Chinese. Name the reply that the whole room, including the man, the rulebook and the papers, understands.
hints: The reply moves understanding from the man to something larger.
It is named after what the man, the book and the papers form together.
questions.onCorrect: The systems reply: understanding belongs to the whole room, not to the man alone.

misconceptions.feedback: That names the thought experiment or another reply. The one wanted moves understanding from the man to something larger.

questions.prompt: Two machines, one of gears and one of silicon chips, share the same machine table and receive the same coins. Do they end in different functional states? Answer yes or no.
hints: A functional state is defined by its place in the table.
Does the table mention gears or chips?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. Functional states are fixed by the table, which is identical; only the realisers differ.

questions.onCorrect: No. The table is identical, so the functional states are too. Only the realisers differ.

misconceptions.feedback: A functional state is fixed by its place in the table. Does the table mention gears or chips?

questions.prompt: What conclusion does Searle draw from the Chinese Room?
hints: Searle grants that the room's replies are fluent.

acceptedIdeas: Running a program is not by itself sufficient for understanding
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Searle grants the behaviour. He denies that implementing the program is enough for understanding.

choices.label: Running a program is not by itself sufficient for understanding
No computer can ever behave as if it understands
Only biological brains can run programs

questions.onCorrect: Searle grants the fluent behaviour and denies that running a program is enough for understanding.

misconceptions.feedback: Searle grants that the room's replies are fluent. His claim is about what running a program amounts to.
He makes no claim about which things can run programs. His claim is about what running one amounts to.

questions.prompt: Both calculators show 7. Are they both adding? Answer yes or no.
hints: What makes something an adder: its parts, or what it does with its inputs?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes. Adding is what each does with 3 and 4, whatever its parts are.

questions.onCorrect: Yes. What counts is what each does with its inputs, whatever it is built from.

misconceptions.feedback: Both turn the same inputs into the same output by following the same rules. Does it matter what the parts are made of?

questions.prompt: In the drinks machine, what does “10p credited” mean?
hints: The table says what each state does, not what it is made of.

acceptedIdeas: The state that turns a further 10p into a can
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The state that turns a further 10p into a can

choices.label: The state that turns a further 10p into a can
A particular metal part inside the machine
A 10p coin sitting in the tray

questions.onCorrect: The state is defined by its role in the table: what it does with the next coin.

misconceptions.feedback: The table never mentions parts. A state is defined by what it does next.
A coin is an input, not a state. The state is defined by what it does with the next input.

questions.prompt: Why does the machine's response to a 10p depend on its state?
hints: Compare what a 10p does from nothing owed with what it does from 10p credited.

acceptedIdeas: The same coin does different things in different states.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The same coin does different things in different states.

choices.label: The same coin does different things in different states.
Coins vary from one to the next.
It counts how many cans it has sold.

questions.onCorrect: The table pairs each state with each input. The same coin can start a credit or complete a sale.

misconceptions.feedback: Every 10p is treated alike. Compare what it does in different states.
